newsitem.title: USA: Democrats, Republicans seek new party chairmen.
newsitem.headline: Democrats, Republicans seek new party chairmen.

text.p: Help wanted signs are out for new chairmen of the Republican and Democratic parties. Job duties are similar but tasks differ as President Bill Clinton's Democrats try to get out of a controversy over foreign donations.
Haley Barbour, chairman of the Republican National Committee -- organisational title of the party -- is leaving after four years.

So are co-chairmen of the Democratic National Committee, national chairman Don Fowler and the general chairman, Sen. Christopher Dodd of Connecticut, after two years. This time Democrats are expected to elect a single chairman.

New party chiefs will be elected at separate meetings of state committeemen and women and state party chairmen in January. Women are being mentioned as possible candidates to head each party for the first time since the 1970s.

If parties actually advertised, they might say: "Wanted: Savvy chief of national party. Duties: Win elections. Raise money. Orchestrate 50 state parties. Must endure long hours, travel, many handshakes, rubber chicken circuit and heat of media scrutiny. Equal Opportunity Employer."

If a help ad were really posted, what would it say? An unsuccessful Republican presidential nominee, former Tennessee Gov. Lamar Alexander, suggested one for his party: "Wanted -- choral director. Someone skilled at leading a slightly out-of-tune, short of practice, group of men and women who are singing the right songs but who have not yet learned to perform it well enough to attract a majority audience."
The salary's not bad, equal to the congressional salary of $133,600 for the Democratic chairman and presumably the Republican, although Republicans will not reveal it.
Barbour, the drawling Yazoo, Miss., lawyer and one-time White House political director, is leaving with mixed results.
When he took over in 1993 the party was at a low ebb. Democrat Clinton had just beaten Republican President George Bush. Democrats kept control of both the House and Senate.
But in two years, party fortunes rose dramatically when both houses of Congress went Republican for the first time in 40 years and the party picked up governors and state legislatures.
Last week's election was a split decision. Clinton beat Republican Bob Dole, but Republicans kept control of Congress, losing some seats in the House but gaining two in the Senate.

Current goals of both party chairmen ahead are to win the only two governors' races in 1997 -- in New Jersey and Virginia -- and fight for congressional seats, governors and state elections in the 1998 mid-presidential term elections.

But Democrats face an immediate formidable challenge in trying to extricate themselves from the growing controversy over questionable contributions to the party from donors with ties to Indonesia, Taiwan and other foreign interests.

At the centre of investigations by the Justice Department, Commerce Department Inspector General, the Democratic committee itself and expected probes by Republicans in Congress is John Huang, a former Democratic fundraiser.

Huang is a former executive with the Indonesia-based Lippo Group, an international financial conglomerate, who left to become a Deputy Assistant Secretary of Commerce for 13 months in 1994 and 1995. He then became a Democratic fundraiser who raised some $2.5 million from Asian-Americans and others.
But after reports of alleged improper contributions, the party in recent weeks returned some $762,000.
Since Clinton is also leader of the party, he likely will handpick a new chairman. One name being mentioned is Terry McAuliffe, the Clinton campaign finance chairman.

Others bandied about include former Texas Gov. Ann Richards, Florida Sen. Bob Graham, California Sen. Dianne Feinstein, party vice chairman Debra DeLee and Louisiana Sen. John Breaux, although Breaux indicated he will not run.

Republicans mentioned include Michigan state chairman, Elisabeth Betsy Devos, a manufacturing business president, and Michigan national committeeman Charles Yob, president of a distributor of industrial conveyer belts.
One hot candidate, former Minnesota Representative Vin Weber, told Reuters "I've been talked about but I'm not going to do it.

Others include outgoing New Hampshire Gov. Steve Merrill, New York party chairman Bill Powers, former Energy Secretary John Herrington, Florida chairman Tom Slade, Ohio chairman Robert Bennett and New Jersey committeeman David Norcross.
